s1.essay:
The play opens in the dark, outside the gates, with two sisters whispering, and inside a hundred lines they are finished with each other. That speed is what I notice first. Antigone has not come to consult Ismene. She has come to test her: 'now ’tis thine to show / If thou art worthy of thy blood or base' is an ultimatum that only looks like news. The decision to bury Polyneices was made before the first line, and we never see her make it.

So the scene's real argument belongs to Ismene, and I think it is a better argument than its reputation. She counts the family dead, father, mother, both brothers, and asks whether the two who remain must go the same way. She does not say Creon is right. She asks 'the dead to pardon' her, which concedes that the dead are owed something, and pleads force: 'the stronger rules.' Storr closes her speech with a rhymed couplet about 'the golden mean,' a Horatian tag that makes her sound more complacent than she is. What she is really saying is that she is frightened and has cause to be.

Antigone's answer is the first sign of how odd she is. 'How sweet to die in such employ' is not the voice of someone accepting a risk. She wants the death almost as much as the burial, and she pictures it as rest beside her brother, 'linked in love’s embrace.' Then she turns on her sister for offering secrecy: tell everyone, she says, or I shall hate thee more. The burial is meant to be seen. Whatever else it is, it is a public act against a public order, and Creon will not be wrong in [[s5]] to hear it that way.

I keep hold of two small things from this scene. The penalty is stoning, a death the whole city deals out; watch what becomes of that in [[s7]]. And the last line is Ismene's. Thrown off, insulted, called base, she still says her sister is dear to those who love her. Antigone leaves without answering.

annotations.quote: The weird of Oedipus, a world of woes!
annotations.note: 'Weird' is a noun here, the old word for fate or doom, as in the Weird Sisters. Antigone's first thought is that she lives inside a family curse, and the elders will sing the same idea back at her in the Second Stasimon.

annotations.quote: Whoe’er transgresses shall be stoned to death.
annotations.note: Stoning is an execution in which the community takes part. Creon will quietly swap it for something more private later, and I think the swap tells us he has stopped trusting the community to throw.

annotations.quote: What right has he to keep me from my own?
annotations.note: This is her whole case in nine words, and notice that it is not yet about heaven. Polyneices is hers. The grand language about unwritten laws comes later; the possessive comes first.

annotations.quote: Not framed by nature to contend with men.
annotations.note: Ismene states as a fact of nature the very thing Creon will keep repeating as a fear. The play lets a woman say it first, gently, before a man says it with guards behind him.

annotations.quote: A sinless sinner, banned awhile on earth,
annotations.note: Storr is rendering a famous Greek oxymoron, something like 'having committed a holy crime.' She knows it is a crime. She never pretends the law does not exist, only that a higher one outranks it.

annotations.quote: If thou proclaim it not to all the town.
annotations.note: The moment that complicates any reading of her as a private mourner. She wants witnesses. Secrecy would save her life and she treats the suggestion as an insult.

annotations.quote: Yet to thy lovers thou art dear as ever.
annotations.note: 'Lovers' means simply those who love her, her own people. It is a generous exit line from the sister who has just been told she is hated, and it goes unanswered.

links.why: Ismene comes back and tries to claim a share in the deed she refuses here, and Antigone's reply is harder than anything in this scene.
'How sweet to die' meets the actual walk to the tomb, and it does not sound sweet any more.
Creon delivers in public, with his reasons, the edict the sisters have only heard by rumour.

s2.essay:
After the sisters' whispering in the dark, the old men of Thebes walk on and greet the sun. It is a real pleasure of the play's construction: private night, then public morning. The elders have just lived through a siege, and their song is the relief of people who expected to be dead or enslaved by now. The enemy army becomes one great white eagle screaming over the walls, and Zeus knocks it out of the sky.

What I notice is where Polyneices sits in this picture. For the elders he is the cause of the eagle, the man whose 'claim' brought a foreign host to burn their towers. They are not thinking of him as anyone's brother. When the brothers do appear, they get four lines at the end of a stanza and the tone goes quiet: one mother, one father, each killed by the other. Then straight back to victory.

And they want to forget. 'Memories of war blot out' is the truest line in the ode, and the play will not let them. The thing they most want to stop thinking about is lying unburied outside the walls and will be the only subject of the day.

Two practical notes on this printing. 'Great Area' is Ares, and 'festal should' is surely 'festal shout'; the text has a few slips like these. And notice that they call on Bacchus to lead the dance. They do it once more, in [[s12]], and both times bad news is already on its way.

annotations.quote: To vindicate fell Polyneices’ claim.
annotations.note: 'Fell' means cruel or deadly. But 'claim' gives something away: in the legend the brothers were to share the throne and Eteocles kept it. The elders' own song admits the traitor had a grievance.

annotations.quote: Forced by the Dragon; in their rear
annotations.note: The Dragon is Thebes itself. The city's first men were said to have sprung from dragon's teeth sown in the ground, so the Thebans are the serpent's brood and the Argive eagle has met its natural enemy.

annotations.quote: Drave, and both perished, brother slain by brother.
annotations.note: 'Drave' is the old past tense of drive. This is all the victory ode has to say about the event that made Creon king and that drives the whole play: one line, then on to the dancing.

annotations.quote: Crowned by this strange chance, our king.
annotations.note: A cool way to announce a monarch. Creon holds the throne by accident, because both heirs died yesterday. Everything he does in the next scene is done by a man one day into the job and anxious to look equal to it.

links.why: The second hymn to Bacchus, sung in hope just before the catastrophe, answers this one sung in relief just before the trouble starts.
The same Polyneices the elders picture as an eagle is the corpse Creon now legislates about.

s3.essay:
Creon's first speech is good, and it should be allowed to be good. He does not come on as a tyrant. He comes on as a man who has inherited a city one day after it nearly burned, and who says, sensibly, that nobody knows what a ruler is made of 'till he be proved by exercise of power.' His principle is that the city is the ship everyone sails in, and that a man who puts a friend before it is contemptible. A century later Demosthenes quoted these lines to an Athenian jury as a model of what a statesman ought to think. Polyneices led a foreign army against his own walls. Refusing him honours is not madness.

But listen to how the elders receive it. 'Thy word is law; thou canst dispose of us.' That is assent without agreement. They say he has the power, and they do not say he is right, and when he asks them to help enforce the order they suggest he find younger men. The speech about the ship of state has landed on people who are already keeping their heads down.

Then the Guard arrives, and the play turns briefly into comedy. He has argued with himself the whole way, he wants it on record that he neither did it nor saw it done, and he has to be told to shoot his bolt and go. I like him a great deal. He is what people are actually like under a threat, and he is there so that we can measure Antigone against the usual thing.

His news is strange. The body is covered with dust, there are no tracks, and no animal has touched it. The elders wonder aloud whether a god did this, and Creon explodes. That explosion is the first crack. He knows, he says, that the gods could have no thought for this dead man, and since it cannot be the gods it must be money: malcontents have bribed the guards. He has no evidence. He reaches for bribery again when the prophet comes in [[s11]]. A man who can explain every opposition as corruption never has to ask whether the opposition has a point.

annotations.quote: Till he be proved by exercise of power;
annotations.note: Creon sets the terms of his own examination in his first minute on stage. The rest of the play is the test he asks for here, and he fails it by his own standard.

annotations.quote: Farewell to friendship, if she suffers wreck.
annotations.note: The ship of state is his favourite image and an honourable one. The word doing the damage is 'friend': the Greek word covers kin and loved ones too, so he is ranking family below the city before he knows the offender is his niece.

annotations.quote: For dogs and carrion crows, a ghastly sight.
annotations.note: The point of the order is the sight. He is not only withholding honour, he is making an exhibit, and it is the exhibit, the flesh carried about by birds, that the gods will answer.

annotations.quote: Thy word is law; thou canst dispose of us
annotations.note: Read this coldly. The elders describe his power and decline to praise his judgment. Antigone will claim in the next episode that the city agrees with her and is afraid to say so; this line is quiet support for her.

annotations.quote: Thus leisurely I hastened on my road;
annotations.note: A lovely comic contradiction, and Storr gets it into five words. The Guard is the only person in the play who is funny, and his dithering is the play's picture of ordinary fear.

annotations.quote: No sign that human hands had been at work.
annotations.note: The play never fully explains this first burial. A light scattering of dust, no tracks, the animals kept off: the elders think of the gods at once, and Sophocles leaves the door open.

annotations.quote: That gods would have a thought for this dead man?
annotations.note: Here Creon stops speaking for the city and starts speaking for heaven. He is sure he knows whom the gods despise. Teiresias exists in this play to tell him he does not.

annotations.quote: Alas! how sad when reasoners reason wrong.
annotations.note: The lowest person on stage tells the king, accurately, that he has reasoned his way to a false conclusion. Creon hears only insolence. It is the first of several true things he will be told by people he outranks.

links.why: The Guard swears he will never come back and returns almost at once with the culprit.
Creon's reflex here, that opposition means bribery, is repeated word for word against the prophet.
The ship of state and the fear of disorder get their fullest and most damaging statement to Haemon.

s4.essay:
This is the most famous ode in Greek tragedy, and it is odd that it is here. The elders have just heard that someone has defied the king and left no trace, and what they sing is a hymn to human cleverness: man crosses the sea, wears down the earth with ploughs, snares birds, breaks horses, teaches himself speech and cities and shelter. Storr sets it in long rhymed lines that roll like a Victorian hymn, and it is easy to hear it as plain praise.

It is not plain praise. The Greek word behind 'wondrous' also means terrible, formidable, uncanny; the first line could as fairly run 'many things are fearsome, and nothing more fearsome than man.' Read it that way and the catalogue darkens. Everything in it is something being mastered, the eldest of the gods included. And the list ends on its one exception: 'for death he hath found no cure.' The play is about a corpse and is heading for a tomb, and the ode has just named the one power nobody on stage can legislate.

The last stanza turns to judgment. Cleverness goes either way; the man who keeps the laws stands high in his city, and the bold transgressor is 'cityless.' The elders mean whoever buried the body. I think the description fits Creon at least as well, and by [[s13]] he is the one with no city worth having. Then, as if to mock the song about man the tamer, the Guard walks in with a girl.

annotations.quote: Many wonders there be, but naught more wondrous than man;
annotations.note: The Greek adjective means awe-inspiring in both directions, marvellous and dreadful. 'Wondrous' keeps only the sunny half. Keep the other half in mind and the ode becomes a warning.

annotations.quote: And the eldest of deities Earth that knows not toil nor decay
annotations.note: Even Earth, a goddess older than Zeus, is something man 'furrows and scores.' It is also earth, a handful of dust, that has just been scattered on Polyneices. The ode and the crime share a substance.

annotations.quote: Safe whate’er may befall: yet for death he hath found no cure.
annotations.note: The hinge of the ode. After five stanzas of mastery, one clause of limit. Creon is about to use death as an instrument of policy, twice, and learn that it does not stay where it is put.

annotations.quote: Proudly his city shall stand; but a cityless outcast I rate
annotations.note: The Greek sets two coined-sounding words side by side, 'high in his city' and 'without a city.' The elders think they are describing a criminal. They have described the alternatives open to their king.

links.why: The man who ends 'a cipher, less than nothing' is the cityless figure this ode imagines, and it is not the one the elders meant.
The next ode drops this confidence in human skill entirely and sings of a family that nothing can save.

s5.essay:
The Guard is back, 'forsworn' and cheerful, and before the great argument begins he gives the best piece of description in the play. They brushed the dust off the body and sat upwind of the smell. At noon a whirlwind blotted out the sky, and when it cleared the girl was standing there, crying 'as when the mother bird beholds her nest / Robbed of its nestlings.' She then poured the offering three times and did not run. The Guard is 'glad—and grieved,' and concludes that a man's first duty is to himself. It is exactly the principle Antigone lacks, stated by a decent man with no shame about it.

Then Creon asks whether she knew the law, and she says 'I knew, all knew,' and makes the speech the play is remembered for. Look closely at what it claims. She does not say that conscience outranks the State, or that she may break any law she dislikes. She says something narrower: that the care of the dead belongs to the gods below, that their rules 'were not born today nor yesterday,' and that a mortal cannot 'by a breath annul' them. It is a claim about jurisdiction. Creon governs the living city. The corpse has passed out of it.

Creon's side deserves a fair hearing, and the stichomythia, the rapid line-for-line exchange, gives it one. Eteocles died defending the walls his brother came to burn. 'Why cast a slur on one by honoring one?' is a real question. If the defender and the attacker receive the same rites, what has the city said about the difference between them? Athens itself refused traitors burial in home soil. And Creon is doing the thing we normally ask of a magistrate: he will not make an exception because the offender is his sister's child. On the day after a civil war, a ruler who let his own household flout the first order of his reign would be inviting the next war.

The usual grand reading, Hegel's, is that this is right against right, family against State, each justified and each one-sided. I think that is half true, and I do not land in the middle. Both are defending something real. But Antigone answers his best question with a line he cannot touch: 'Who knows if this world’s crimes are virtues there?' She is saying that the city's categories of patriot and outlaw may not apply where her brother now is, and that Creon is legislating in a country he has never seen. And listen to what happens to his reasons as he loses. He begins with the law and ends with 'I am woman, she the man' and 'No woman shall be the master while I live.' What started as the city's safety has become his own standing. The gods of this play side with her before it is over. So do I, on the deed. Refusing a traitor a hero's funeral was within a ruler's gift. Keeping the body above ground as a spectacle, and killing whoever covers it, reaches past the city into ground no king holds. And an order that the lawgiver's own niece, son and prophet must each in turn break or protest is, at the least, a badly made law.

On the person I am less sure, and the Ismene scene is why. Ismene comes out and lies to share her sister's death: 'I did the deed, if she will have it so.' It is the bravest thing she does, and Antigone refuses it flat. 'A friend in word is never friend of mine.' The woman who has just said her nature is for love and not hate cannot find any for the sister standing in front of her. Some of it may be rescue; 'save thyself; I grudge not thy escape' can be heard as protection. Some of it is plain pride of ownership in the deed. 'Thou livest, I died long ago' is the coldest line in the scene, and it is true.

One more thing surfaces only now, and from Ismene: Antigone is engaged to Creon's son. She has not thought it worth mentioning.

annotations.quote: As when the mother bird beholds her nest
annotations.note: The only tender image anyone gives her, and it comes from the man arresting her. It also makes her a mother at the moment she gives up any chance of being one, a loss she will count over in the Kommos.

annotations.quote: A man’s first duty is to serve himself.
annotations.note: The Guard's creed, offered without embarrassment. Set it beside the next thing anyone says to Creon and the distance between an ordinary person and Antigone is measured exactly.

annotations.quote: Guilty. I did it, I deny it not.
annotations.note: Creon has told her to speak with bowed head. She answers in three flat statements. There will be no trial because she has taken the question of fact off the table; only the question of right is left.

annotations.quote: The immutable unwritten laws of Heaven.
annotations.note: The phrase that made the play a founding text for every later argument about higher law. Notice how specific she is being: these are the rites owed to the dead, not a general licence for conscience.

annotations.quote: This ill-starred maiden kicks against the pricks.
annotations.note: Storr borrows the phrase from the King James Bible, where it describes an ox kicking the goad and hurting only itself. The elders file her under her father's temperament, which spares them an opinion on her argument.

annotations.quote: Unpunished, I am woman, she the man.
annotations.note: The first time Creon says what is really at stake for him. It is not in his opening speech about the ship of state. From here on he says it in nearly every scene.

annotations.quote: Who knows if this world’s crimes are virtues there?
annotations.note: Her best line of argument and her most modest. She does not claim to know the mind of the dead. She says he does not either, and that he is punishing on the assumption that he does.

annotations.quote: My nature is for mutual love, not hate.
annotations.note: The Greek uses two verbs she seems to coin for the occasion: I was born to join in loving, not to join in hating. It is the line everyone remembers, and within a minute she is refusing her sister.

annotations.quote: O Haemon, how thy sire dishonors thee!
annotations.note: The only time she speaks his name, if she speaks it at all. The manuscripts give this line to Ismene, and many editors, Storr among them, move it to Antigone because it seems too warm to leave her silent. I can believe it either way.

links.why: Ismene's refusal before dawn is the thing Antigone will not let her take back here.
Haemon confirms what Antigone asserts in this scene, that the city thinks as she does and holds its breath.
The certainty of the unwritten-laws speech gives way to doubt and to a far stranger argument.
Teiresias settles the question of jurisdiction she raises: the dead and the gods below are not Creon's to command.

s6.essay:
The confidence of the last ode is gone. There the elders sang of what man can do; here they sing of a family for whom doing makes no difference. Once heaven's curse touches a house, trouble passes from generation to generation like a sea driven by the north wind, 'billow on billow.' It is the best image in the ode, and its cold, heavy rhythm survives even Storr's rhyming quatrains.

I read this as the elders finding a way not to judge. They have just watched their king condemn two girls, and what they offer is an explanation by inheritance: she is a daughter of Labdacus's line, the last shoot of a doomed tree, so of course this is happening. The Greek speaks of light spreading over the last root of the house, meaning the sisters; Storr's 'last born son' blurs that. Either way, nobody is responsible. Fate did it.

Then the ode lifts to Zeus, whom neither sleep nor time can touch, and comes down on a proverb about hope and delusion: when evil starts to look good to a man, ruin is close. They are thinking of Antigone, who called her death a gain. But who in this play mistakes a harm for a good and cannot be told otherwise? This is the pattern I find in every ode: aimed at her, it lands on Creon. He is about to prove it at length with his son.

annotations.quote: The infection lingers on and speeds apace,
annotations.note: The curse as contagion in the blood. It is the same idea Antigone opened the play with, the 'weird of Oedipus,' but from her it was a grievance and from the elders it is an excuse.

annotations.quote: Laid on the race a malison, and his rod
annotations.note: 'Malison' is the opposite of benison: a curse. The house is that of Labdacus, grandfather of Oedipus, and the elders do not say which god or why. The vagueness is the point; nobody can be blamed.

annotations.quote: All that exceeds the mean by Fate
annotations.note: The elders' whole moral philosophy in one line: do not be excessive. It suits old men who have survived several kings. It has nothing to say about what to do when the moderate course is to leave a brother to the dogs.

annotations.quote: Till ’neath his feet the treacherous ashes burn.
annotations.note: A man walking over ground he thinks is cold. They mean it for Antigone, but she knew exactly what she was walking on. The one who does not feel the heat yet is Creon.

links.why: Set this beside the ode to human ingenuity sung one scene earlier; the elders' mood has turned completely.
Antigone takes up the family curse herself on the way to the tomb, and it is her 'most poignant pain,' not a theory.

s7.essay:
Haemon begins with a submission so complete, 'O father, I am thine,' that I cannot tell whether it is sincere or tactical, and I suspect he could not either. Creon takes it at face value and delivers his fullest statement of what he believes. Much of it is still reasonable. A man who cannot govern his household will not govern a city; an army holds only while discipline holds; these people were under siege two days ago. Then he says the thing that loses the argument: whoever the State appoints must be obeyed in everything, 'just and unjust alike.' He has stopped claiming the edict is right. He is claiming that it need not be.

Haemon's reply is a model of how to tell a powerful man he is wrong. He does not plead for his bride. He never once says he loves her. He reports, as a loyal son who hears what a king cannot, that the city is mourning the girl and thinks her name should be 'writ in gold.' So Antigone was right in [[s5]] about those bated breaths. Then come two pictures of bending: trees that give way to a flood and keep their twigs, a sailor who will not slacken the sheet and goes over.

None of it gets through, because Creon can only hear a boy besotted with a woman. The quick exchange that follows is the political heart of the play. 'A State for one man is no State at all.' 'The State is his who rules it.' That second line is where the ship of state from [[s3]] ends up. Then Haemon says one will die with her, meaning himself, and his father hears a threat on his own life.

Two small decisions close the scene, and both tell on Creon. Asked whether he really means to kill both sisters, he says 'I stand corrected' and spares Ismene in half a line; he can change his mind when nothing rides on it. And the stoning announced in [[s1]] becomes a cave with a little food, so that technically no one has killed her. It is a lawyer's device for avoiding pollution, and Teiresias will see straight through it.

annotations.quote: Know’st not whate’er we do is done in love?
annotations.note: Creon's first move is to ask for trust in advance. He means it; he does love his son. The line is unbearable on a second reading.

annotations.quote: But small and great, just and unjust alike.
annotations.note: 'But' looks like a slip in this printing for 'Both.' The sentence is the turning point of Creon's case: obedience is owed even to unjust commands. Nothing he said in his opening speech required this, and nothing after it recovers.

annotations.quote: Should not her name (they cry) be writ in gold?
annotations.note: Our only report of what ordinary Thebans think, and it reaches us third-hand through a son with a motive. I believe it anyway, because the elders' chilly 'Thy word is law' pointed the same direction.

annotations.quote: But by resisting perish root and branch.
annotations.note: Haemon's tree. A few minutes ago the elders sang of fate felling the tree of Oedipus's house. Now the image is offered to Creon as a choice he still has.

annotations.quote: A State for one man is no State at all.
annotations.note: An Athenian audience, proud of governing itself, would have gone with this line at once. Haemon has shifted the ground from what his father may forbid to whose city it is.

annotations.quote: As monarch of a desert thou wouldst shine.
annotations.note: The deferential son is gone and this is sarcasm. It is also prophecy. By the end Creon rules a palace with nobody left in it.

annotations.quote: So she shall die, but one will die with her.
annotations.note: He means himself. Creon assumes he is being threatened, since by now he reads every sentence as an attack on his authority. The whole catastrophe is folded into this misunderstanding.

annotations.quote: With food no more than to avoid the taint
annotations.note: The ration is a legal fiction: if she starves with food beside her, the city has not shed kindred blood. Creon, who scoffed at the gods' interest in a corpse, turns out to be careful about ritual when it protects him.

links.why: The messenger's account of the cave is the last meeting of this father and son, and it answers every line of this quarrel.
The elders at once explain the scene as the work of Love, which is to hear it exactly as Creon did.
The ship of state that sounded statesmanlike there becomes 'the State is his who rules it' here.

s8.essay:
The shortest ode in the play, and the elders' quickest verdict. They have just listened to a young man argue, carefully and politically, that a ruler should heed his people, and what they conclude is that Love did it. Love is unbeatable, Love sends the wisest mad, Love 'didst kindle the strife, this feud of kinsman with kin.' That is Creon's own reading of his son, a boy turned by a woman, set to music.

I think they are wrong about Haemon, who talked about justice and the city and never about desire. But the ode is truer than they intend. Something like love is behind every act in this story: Antigone's for a brother, which she called her nature; Haemon's, which he will prove in the only way left to him; even Creon's for the son he is about to lose. The elders name a god to dismiss a quarrel and name the engine of the play instead.

Then Antigone is brought out under guard and the song breaks off. 'Lo I myself am borne aside' is as close as these cautious men come to confessing that the sight of her undoes their loyalty to the edict. Storr has them swept 'from Justice'; the Greek is nearer to being carried outside the ordinances, past what they are allowed to feel. They weep. They still do nothing. And 'Death’s bower,' a bridal chamber, sets the figure for the scene that follows.

annotations.quote: Love who pillowed all night on a maiden’s cheek dost lie,
annotations.note: The one soft picture in a hard ode: Love asleep on a girl's cheek. The Greek names Eros, and later Aphrodite; Storr makes both 'Love.' The girl we are about to see has no such nights ahead.

annotations.quote: Thou didst kindle the strife, this feud of kinsman with kin,
annotations.note: The elders' diagnosis of the father-son quarrel. It lets them avoid asking which of the two was right, a question they answered a moment ago by saying both had spoken well.

annotations.quote: Lo I myself am borne aside,
annotations.note: The elders have just sung that Love sweeps men off the path of right, and now they are swept too, by pity. It is their most honest line so far, and it changes nothing they do.

links.why: This ode is the elders' reading of the quarrel just ended, and it is worth checking against what Haemon actually said.
The bridal chamber of Death, named in the ode's last line, becomes Antigone's own refrain.

s9.essay:
The woman who told Creon that death was gain now turns for 'one last fond, lingering, longing look' at the sun. I do not think this is inconsistency, and it is not Sophocles weakening her. It is the difference between defying a death sentence and walking to the place. For the first time she is not arguing with anyone, and what comes out is grief for an ordinary life: no wedding song, no flowers on the bed, no children. She never names Haemon, here or anywhere. What she mourns is marriage itself, the thing every girl in her city was raised to expect, and she sings of it in the lyric metres of a lament. She is conducting her own funeral because nobody else will.

The elders are worse than useless. They tell her she goes 'great and glorious,' that no disease has wasted her, that she alone descends alive. The Greek behind 'freely' is the word that gives us autonomous: she goes by her own law. It is meant as a tribute and she hears it as a taunt. 'Ye mock me.' When she reaches for Niobe, the grieving queen turned to weeping stone, they correct her: Niobe was a goddess and you are not. Then they return to her father, and to their real position: piety is all very well, but power is power, and she was 'a self-willed rebel.' These are the citizens Haemon said were on her side. They are, and this is what their sympathy is worth.

Creon comes in to hurry things, and his speech is a small masterpiece of hand-washing. She is to be left 'at liberty to die, / Or, if she choose, to live in solitude.' 'We in either case / Are guiltless.' He has persuaded himself that walling a girl in a cave is not killing her. Set this beside her 'Guilty. I did it, I deny it not' in [[s5]]. She owned her act in a single line before the whole city. He, with all the power, arranges his so that it will have no author. Of the two, she is the one behaving like a ruler.

Then comes her last speech, and the passage that has embarrassed admirers for two centuries. She says she would not have done this for a husband or a child. A husband can be replaced, another child can be born, but with both parents dead 'no second brother can be born for me.' Goethe wished some scholar would prove the lines spurious. They echo a story in Herodotus about a Persian woman allowed to save one relative. But Aristotle quotes them, so they were in the play he knew, and I have come round to keeping them.

My reason is this. The argument is bad; it is a sum, and it shrinks the 'unwritten laws of Heaven' to a rule about one kind of kinship. But look at where she is. Everyone has left her, the elders have just called her a rebel, and no god has given any sign. She reaches for a reason that might convince the people in front of her and comes up with a borrowed, clumsy one. People do this. And clumsy as it is, it tells the truth she told in the first scene, before the fine language: 'What right has he to keep me from my own?' It was always this brother. Storr softens it by calling her rule 'the law of conscience'; as far as I can tell the Greek says only 'such a law,' and conscience is his century's word, not hers.

What I find hardest is what follows. 'What ordinance of heaven have I transgressed?' She does not know. If the gods approve of this, she says, she will learn her sin by suffering; if the sin is Creon's, let him suffer no more than she has. She goes into the rock without her answer. It arrives in [[s11]], spoken to someone else, after she is past hearing it. That is why I call her brave and not merely certain.

annotations.quote: One last fond, lingering, longing look I take
annotations.note: Storr piles up three adjectives where the Greek is spare, and for once the Victorian excess seems right to me. This is the same woman who called death sweet, and she cannot take her eyes off the daylight.

annotations.quote: Living to the dead below.
annotations.note: The elders offer this as her distinction. It is in fact the horror of the sentence: she will be neither buried nor alive. Creon has left one corpse above ground and is sending one living body under it.

annotations.quote: Chained upon Siphylus’ high rocky fell,
annotations.note: Tantalus's child is Niobe, who boasted of her children, lost them all, and turned to stone on Mount Sipylus, still weeping. A 'fell' is a bare hillside. Antigone, who will have no children, picks the great mourning mother as her likeness.

annotations.quote: Alack, alack! Ye mock me. Is it meet
annotations.note: 'Meet' means fitting. She came out wanting mourners and got a comparison corrected. This is the only time in the play she asks anyone for anything, and they fail her.

annotations.quote: And alien midst the living and the dead.
annotations.note: The Greek word is the one Athenians used for a resident foreigner, someone who lives in a city without belonging to it. She says she will be that everywhere, at home neither above nor below.

annotations.quote: Thou a father’s guild dost bear.
annotations.note: 'Guild' is a misprint for 'guilt.' The elders go back to their explanation from the Second Stasimon, the family curse, and this time they say it to her face. She answers that it is her sharpest pain.

annotations.quote: Leave her alone at liberty to die,
annotations.note: 'At liberty' is grotesque, and I think Sophocles means it to be. Creon is arranging matters so the choice to die will look like hers. In the event she takes him at his word.

annotations.quote: No second brother can be born for me.
annotations.note: The centre of the disputed passage. As reasoning it is thin. As a statement of fact about the house of Oedipus, with father, mother and both brothers dead, it is simply how alone she is.

annotations.quote: Alas, my piety is impious deemed.
annotations.note: The paradox from the first scene, the 'sinless sinner,' now turned inside out and spoken without defiance. Then she owned the crime and boasted of the holiness. Now she has only the verdict.

links.why: Read the unwritten-laws speech again beside this one; the same woman, with the same act behind her, and none of the certainty.
'How sweet to die' and 'What right has he to keep me from my own?' are both answered here, the first by her fear and the second by the brother argument.
The sign from the gods that she asks for and does not get is delivered to Creon by Teiresias.
She predicts she will go unwept, and in the final scene nobody on stage speaks her name.

s10.essay:
Antigone has been led off, and the elders sing to her back. What they offer is precedent: three stories of people shut away. Danae, locked in a bronze chamber by her father; Lycurgus, the Thracian king who mocked Dionysus and was penned in rock; and a third, told so obliquely that a first-time reader may not see it is a story at all, about two boys blinded by a stepmother on the wild coast of Thrace, and their mother, a daughter of the North Wind.

I find this the hardest ode to read, and I do not think that is only Storr. The elders seem not to know what they mean. Danae was innocent, and Zeus came to her in her cell; is that comfort? Lycurgus was a ruler punished for insulting a god; that is a portrait of Creon, not of the girl they are addressing. The third story is plain atrocity inside a family, with a weaving tool for a weapon. The only thread they draw themselves is that birth protects no one. 'Strange are the ways of Fate.'

So the ode is consolation from men who have no position. They twice call her 'my child,' tenderly, now that she cannot hear them and tenderness costs nothing. Meanwhile the stage is filling with the play's vocabulary of sight: a lightless cell, 'sightless orbits.' The next person through the door is a blind man.

annotations.quote: Of Zeus descending in a golden shower.
annotations.note: Danae's father shut her up because of a prophecy that her son would kill him; Zeus reached her anyway as a rain of gold and she bore Perseus. Her prison became a bridal chamber in fact. Antigone's is one only in metaphor.

annotations.quote: ’Twas madness gibes against a god to fling.
annotations.note: Lycurgus, 'Dryas' child,' tried to drive Dionysus and his women out of Thrace. A king shut in rock for scoffing at a god: within minutes Creon will be scoffing at Zeus's eagles to a prophet's face.

annotations.quote: The gore that trickled from a spindle red,
annotations.note: The stepmother put out the boys' eyes with a spindle or shuttle, a household tool turned weapon. The ode never names their mother, Cleopatra, daughter of Boreas. Sophocles' audience knew the tale; we have to piece it together.

annotations.quote: A child of gods; yet she, my child, like thee,
annotations.note: The whole moral, such as it is: even the granddaughter of a god was overtaken. Hear how the address has softened. In the last scene they called her a self-willed rebel.

links.why: The ode's blinded boys and dark cells hand over directly to the blind prophet who sees what Creon cannot.
Antigone chose her own mythical likeness, Niobe, and the elders rejected it; these are the ones they prefer.

s11.essay:
Teiresias comes on led by a boy, 'two wayfarers as one, / Having betwixt us eyes for one,' and for a few lines he and Creon are old colleagues. Creon has always taken his advice; the prophet has helped him steer the city. It matters that Creon has a record of listening. What we are about to watch is not a man who cannot hear, but a man who has stopped hearing today.

The report is horrible and precise. The birds are screaming and tearing one another. The sacrifice will not burn; the fat slides off the thigh bones and the gall bursts. And the cause is physical: the birds and dogs have been feeding on Polyneices and have carried scraps of him to every altar in Thebes. The exhibit Creon ordered in [[s3]] has become the city's pollution. Then Teiresias offers him a way out that costs nothing but pride: 'To err is common / To all men,' and the only fool is the obstinate one.

Creon answers as he answered the Guard. Bribery. Prophets are a money-getting tribe. And then he says the most reckless thing in the play: he will not allow the burial even if Zeus's own eagles carry the carrion up to the god's throne, because 'no human soilure can assail the gods.' As theology that is almost enlightened. In his mouth it is a clever idea put to work for a grudge, and he is saying it to the one man who knows what the gods have just refused.

So Teiresias stops advising and prophesies, and he names the offence more exactly than anyone has: Creon has put a living soul below the earth and kept a dead one above it. Both belong elsewhere. This is Antigone's point about jurisdiction from [[s5]], now made with authority. The price will be a child of his own.

What follows takes about ten lines. The elders, who have not ventured a firm opinion all day, say they have never known this prophet wrong, and Creon folds: 'To yield is grievous.' I find the speed convincing. He was never a monster. He was a man afraid of looking weak, and a larger fear has arrived. Note the order of the elders' instructions, the maiden first and then the tomb, and keep it for [[s13]].

annotations.quote: Having betwixt us eyes for one, we are here.
annotations.note: The blind man who sees truly is an old device, and Sophocles used this same prophet for it again when he came to write of Oedipus. Here the dependence on the boy is stressed: Teiresias knows he needs a guide. Creon does not.

annotations.quote: Thus far I ne’er have disobeyed thy rede.
annotations.note: 'Rede' is counsel. The line gives Creon a past in which he was a sensible ruler who took advice. The play has compressed his fall into one day, and this line shows how far he has travelled since morning.

annotations.quote: And sputtered in the ashes a foul ooze;
annotations.note: Greek sacrifice was supposed to send clean fat-smoke up to the gods. This one will not catch. Storr does not spare us, and he should not: the play insists that the offence is a bodily fact and not a point of etiquette.

annotations.quote: By slaying twice the slain? I mean thee well;
annotations.note: The plainest objection to the edict, and it has taken until now for anyone to voice it: the man is already dead. Whatever punishing a corpse achieves, it is not justice on Polyneices.

annotations.quote: Like anchors at a target; yea, ye set
annotations.note: 'Anchors' is a slip in this printing for 'archers.' Creon feels like a target with everyone shooting at him. Teiresias takes up the image at the end of the scene and tells him these arrows will not miss.

annotations.quote: No human soilure can assail the gods;
annotations.note: 'Soilure' is defilement. The thought, that the gods are too high to be dirtied by us, would be respectable in a philosopher. Creon uses it as permission to go on dirtying their altars.

annotations.quote: And sent below a denizen of earth,
annotations.note: The indictment in one line. A 'denizen of earth' is someone who belongs up here among the living. Creon has reversed the two realms: the living underground, the dead in the sun.

annotations.quote: What should I do. Advise me. I will heed.
annotations.note: The speaker label in this printing says CHORUS, but the line is Creon's; it sits between two speeches of the elders and answers them. It is the first time all day that he has asked anyone what to do.

annotations.quote: Go, free the maiden from her rocky cell;
annotations.note: The living first, then the dead. It is the obvious order, since a corpse can wait and a girl in a cave cannot. Watch what Creon actually does when he gets to the plain.

links.why: Creon met the Guard's news with the same charge of bribery; the habit is the same and this time the witness cannot be frightened.
This is the divine verdict Antigone asked for on her way to the tomb and did not live to hear.
The prophecy of 'life for life' is paid within the hour, and the order in which Creon carries out the elders' advice decides it.

s12.essay:
Creon has run off shouting for axes, and the elders, alone and suddenly hopeful, do what they did at dawn: they call on Bacchus. This is a dance-song, a summons to the city's own god, born of a Theban mother, to come and heal. They chase him over the map, from Italy to Eleusis, Parnassus and its Castalian spring, the vine-covered slopes of Nysa, and bring every stanza home to Thebes, 'thine own.'

It is a beautiful ode and a cruel placement. Sophocles liked to set a burst of joy just before the worst news, and he does it here with complete assurance. The audience knows what a prophet's 'life for life' means. The elders have talked themselves into believing that because the king has changed his mind the story has changed its ending. The Greek asks the god to come 'with cleansing foot'; Storr has only 'Save us, O save!' The next figure to enter is a messenger.

The 'plague' they sing of is the pollution Teiresias described, the sickness of a city whose altars are fouled. And the god they pray to is not a safe one. His followers are a 'maddened rout' who dance all night. Thebes has spent the day learning what happens when a ruler tries to manage the things that belong to the gods, and it ends the day calling on the least manageable god it has.

Slips in this printing: 'All hall' is 'All hail,' and 'thy swift was wending' should be 'thy swift way wending.'

annotations.quote: Thebes, O Bacchus, is thine own.
annotations.note: Dionysus was born of Semele, a Theban princess, which makes him family. The elders are calling in a relative. Compare the dawn ode, where they asked him to lead the victory dance.

annotations.quote: To thee, and to thy Mother levin-stricken,
annotations.note: 'Levin' is an old word for lightning. Semele asked to see Zeus in his true form and was burned up by it. Even the city's patron god comes out of a story about a mortal destroyed by contact with the divine.

annotations.quote: Thou see’st with what a plague our townsfolk sicken.
annotations.note: No epidemic has been mentioned. The plague is the defilement from the unburied body, treated as a disease of the whole city. One man's order has made everyone unclean.

annotations.quote: Leader of all the voices of the night,
annotations.note: A strange and lovely title for a god, and a reminder of how long this one day has run. The play began before sunrise with two sisters. The elders are now asking for an all-night dance that will never take place.

links.why: The entrance song ended with the same god and the same wish to dance, just before Creon came on to announce the edict.
The prayer to be saved is answered at once by the messenger's first words.

s13.essay:
The Messenger begins with a moral before he gives any news, and it is a better one than the play's last lines. Creon had everything, a saved city, a throne, sons, and 'a life / Without life’s joys I count a living death.' That is the sentence Creon passed on Antigone, now passed on him by a servant.

Then Eurydice comes out. We have not seen her before and did not know to expect her. She asks for the story as one 'not unacquaint with misery,' hears all of it, and leaves without a syllable. The elders and the Messenger stand discussing what her silence might mean. I think it the finest stroke of stagecraft in the play: a dozen lines, an exit, and everyone on stage and off knows.

The narrative itself turns on an order of events. The elders told Creon to free the girl and then build the tomb. He does it the other way round. He goes first to the plain, prays, washes what is left of Polyneices, burns it, and heaps 'a mighty mound.' Only then does he go to the cave. I do not think this is carelessness. He is doing the pious thing thoroughly, at last, and the thoroughness kills her. She, for her part, has not waited either. She has hanged herself with her own linen, as her mother did. Haemon is holding her. He looks at his father, spits, draws, lunges, misses, and turns the sword on himself, 'wroth with himself.' The quarrel of [[s7]] ends there without another word between them.

Creon returns carrying the body and says what he could not say all day: 'The fault was mine, mine only.' I believe him, and so do the elders, who answer with the driest line in the play: 'Too late thou seemest to perceive the truth.' The second blow follows at once. Eurydice has died at the altar, cursing him. He begs for death and the elders refuse him even the prayer. He has to go on living, 'a cipher, less than nothing.'

In all this nobody mentions Antigone. Creon mourns his son and his wife and never speaks her name. She said she would go unwept, and the play that is called after her lets that happen. Its closing verse, that wisdom comes to the old through punishment, seems to me small for what we have seen, and I suspect it is meant to be. These elders always did arrive at wisdom a scene behind.

annotations.quote: Without life’s joys I count a living death.
annotations.note: The play's central image changes owners. Antigone was to be the living dead, shut in rock. It is Creon who ends that way, in a palace.

annotations.quote: To one not unacquaint with misery.
annotations.note: Eurydice's only self-description, and it implies a history the play has not told us. She has buried a son already. The Second Messenger fills this in after she is dead.

annotations.quote: And to his memory piled a mighty mound
annotations.note: Polyneices finally gets everything Creon refused him: washing, fire, a barrow. It is done properly and it takes time, and the time is spent while Antigone is alone in the cave.

annotations.quote: A noose of linen twined about her neck;
annotations.note: Ismene described their mother's death in the first scene in nearly the same words, a noose she had twined herself. Antigone ends as Jocasta did. Creon gave her 'liberty to die,' and she used it before he could take it back.

annotations.quote: Wroth with himself, poor wretch, incontinent
annotations.note: 'Incontinent' here means immediately, with no pause. And 'wroth with himself' is exact: he has just tried to kill his father and failed. The suicide is partly love and partly horror at what he nearly did.

annotations.quote: The maid, her pallid cheek incarnadined
annotations.note: Storr reaches for Macbeth's word for staining red. His blood on her white cheek is the only wedding either of them gets, and the Messenger says so in the next lines.

annotations.quote: Is no less ominous than excessive grief.
annotations.note: The elders finally read a situation correctly and in time, and it is still too late to matter. This is the first observation of theirs all day that owes nothing to a proverb.

annotations.quote: She mourned for Megareus who nobly died
annotations.note: The play does not explain this. In the legend another son of Creon died for the city during the siege, and Eurydice plainly holds her husband to account for that death as well. It is the misery she alluded to on entering.

annotations.quote: A cipher, less than nothing; no delay!
annotations.note: A cipher is a zero. In the morning he said that a man is not known until he has held power. By evening he has been known, and this is his own reckoning of the result.

links.why: Every line of the father-son quarrel is answered here: 'one will die with her,' 'never shalt thou again behold my face,' the monarch of a desert.
Teiresias's 'life for life' and the elders' instruction to free the maiden first are both fulfilled, the second in reverse.
Antigone's 'unwept, unwed, unfriended' comes true in this scene, where no one on stage speaks of her.
Creon's inaugural test, that a man is proved by exercise of power, receives its result.
